full_citation: Creedon, C., Bargate, E., Lenney, S., Schofield, M., & Stock, R. (2024). Claims inflation estimation: A practical guide for historical data. Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. https://actuaries.org.uk/media/3i0fik1e/claims-inflation-estimation-a-practical-guide-for-historical-data.pdf
topic: Claims inflation estimation and pseudo-data design
research_question: How can historical claims inflation be estimated, and how do estimation approaches behave when inflation, frequency and development conditions change?
data_used: Controlled pseudo claim data generated under multiple inflation and frequency scenarios; Poisson claim counts, Pareto large-claim severities and a finite development pattern.
methods: Pseudo-data simulation; individual-claim and aggregate inflation diagnostics; scenario-based comparison of claims-inflation estimation approaches.
main_findings: Observed claims data combine severity inflation, frequency change, development and mix effects. Controlled pseudo-data help distinguish genuine inflation from other structural features.
limitations: The scenarios are deliberately simplified and results depend on the assumed data-generating process, development maturity and data quality. The parameter choices are illustrative rather than calibrated to one portfolio.
how_used_in_dissertation: Primary source for the pilot pseudo-data framework and for explaining why inflation, frequency and development effects must be separated.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Literature Review; Chapter 3 – Simulation Methodology
notes: Priority: High. Verified pp. 10–14 and 40–41. p. 11 specifies Poisson mean 50 and a fixed seed; p. 12 specifies Pareto observation point 1,000,000, alpha 2.5 and a ten-development-year pattern; pp. 13–14 define stable, emerging, shock and frequency-trend scenarios. Cite the paper as inspiration, while clearly identifying dissertation-specific changes.

full_citation: Creedon, C., Bargate, E., Lenney, S., Schofield, M., & Stock, R. (2025). Reserving for volatile inflation: A practitioner’s guide to setting best estimate reserves during periods of inflation volatility. Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. https://vle.actuaries.org.uk/pluginfile.php/168696/mod_resource/content/1/Reserving%20During%20Volatile%20Inflation%20v1.9.pdf
research_question: How should best-estimate reserves be adjusted when future claims inflation differs materially from the inflation implicitly embedded in historical triangles?
data_used: Pseudo-data generated across stable, emerging, shock, frequency-trend and inflation-estimation-error scenarios; reserve estimates are compared with known simulated outcomes.
methods: Unadjusted Chain Ladder and Bornhuetter–Ferguson benchmarks; A Priori Uplift; Cashflow Uplift; Management Uplift; Inflation-Adjusted Chain Ladder; discussion of PPCI and PPCF.
main_findings: No single adjustment dominates in every scenario. Unadjusted reserves can be deficient when inflation rises; Cashflow Uplift handles expected reversion more naturally; the paper’s IACL implementation can overstate temporary shocks; severity adjustments do not correct frequency trends.
limitations: The study uses controlled pseudo-data and often assumes strong knowledge of historical and future inflation. Results may differ under real portfolio heterogeneity, parameter uncertainty and operational judgement.
how_used_in_dissertation: Main source for the classical benchmark design and for the stable, emerging and shock inflation comparison.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Literature Review; Chapter 3 – Reserving Methods; Chapter 5 – Discussion
notes: Priority: High. Verified pp. 10–13 for data and scenarios; pp. 15–18 for methods; pp. 20–26 for scenario results; pp. 38–39 for conclusions. Use the paper’s reported errors as literature evidence, not as expected dissertation results.

full_citation: Mack, T. (1993). Distribution-free calculation of the standard error of Chain Ladder reserve estimates. ASTIN Bulletin, 23(2), 213–225. https://doi.org/10.2143/AST.23.2.2005092
topic: Chain Ladder reserving and prediction uncertainty
research_question: How can the standard error of Chain Ladder reserve estimates be calculated without imposing a full parametric distribution on cumulative claims?
data_used: Run-off triangle framework with numerical illustrations.
methods: Classical age-to-age Chain Ladder factors and a distribution-free derivation of reserve standard errors under Mack assumptions.
main_findings: The paper derives practical formulas for process and parameter uncertainty and formalises the stochastic assumptions behind Chain Ladder.
limitations: Requires stable proportional development and independence between accident years. Calendar-year effects can violate independence, and the prediction error does not capture model misspecification or an unprecedented future regime.
how_used_in_dissertation: Foundational citation for the Chain Ladder benchmark, its assumptions and its vulnerability under inflation and structural change.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Classical Reserving; Chapter 3 – Benchmark Model
notes: Priority: High. Article pp. 214–216 set out the conditional-mean and accident-year-independence assumptions. p. 215 explicitly notes calendar-year effects as a possible violation. p. 224 states that the standard error does not capture specification error or future development differing from the past.

full_citation: Creedon, C., Bargate, E., Lenney, S., Schofield, M., & Stock, R. (2025). Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. https://vle.actuaries.org.uk/pluginfile.php/168696/mod_resource/content/1/Reserving%20During%20Volatile%20Inflation%20v1.9.pdf
source_type: Method entry from IFoA practitioner paper
research_question: Can a triangle be put onto a common price basis before Chain Ladder and then re-inflated using forecast calendar-year inflation?
data_used: Incremental paid-claims triangles from controlled volatile-inflation pseudo-data scenarios.
methods: Transform to incremental data; adjust historical cells to a common price basis; rebuild cumulative data; apply Chain Ladder; derive future increments; apply future calendar-year inflation; sum future inflated cells.
main_findings: IACL explicitly separates calendar-year inflation from development. It improves on an unadjusted approach in some rising-inflation cases but can over-reserve when a temporary spike is effectively extrapolated.
limitations: Requires defensible historical and future inflation indices, correct cell-to-calendar-year mapping and stable development after adjustment. Results remain sensitive to the future inflation path.
how_used_in_dissertation: Implemented as a core classical inflation-aware model and compared with unadjusted Chain Ladder, Cashflow Uplift and ML models.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Inflation-Aware Reserving; Chapter 3 – Model Specification
notes: Priority: High. Method steps are on pp. 17–18. Scenario B results are on p. 22 and shock-inflation results on pp. 22–23. Document the precise base year, deflation convention and future re-inflation formula used in Python.

source_type: Method entry from IFoA practitioner paper
research_question: Can projected reserve cashflows be adjusted for the compounded difference between inflation implicit in the baseline reserve and the expected future inflation path?
data_used: Baseline reserve cashflows and payment patterns applied to controlled pseudo-data scenarios.
methods: Produce a baseline reserve and future cashflow pattern; estimate implicit historical inflation; uplift or reduce each future cashflow for the difference between implicit and forecast inflation, compounded to its payment date.
main_findings: The method is transparent, works with existing reserving outputs and can reflect an inflation path that rises and then reverts. In the paper’s shock scenario it was closer to the simulated truth than leaving reserves unadjusted or the paper’s IACL implementation.
limitations: Depends on the quality of the baseline reserve, payment pattern, implicit-inflation estimate and future forecast. It does not itself correct frequency change or settlement-pattern misspecification.
how_used_in_dissertation: Implemented as a separate classical inflation adjustment because its response to temporary inflation differs materially from IACL.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Inflation-Aware Reserving; Chapter 3 – Model Specification
notes: Priority: High. Method is described on pp. 16–17. Scenario B and C comparisons are on pp. 22–23. Define what inflation is already implicit in the baseline reserve and apply the uplift by origin year and payment period.

full_citation: Albrecher, H., Beirlant, J., & Teugels, J. L. (2017). Reinsurance: Actuarial and statistical aspects. Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119412540
research_question: How should reinsurance forms, layer transformations, heavy-tailed losses and pricing quantities be modelled?
data_used: Theoretical loss distributions, actuarial examples and reinsurance applications rather than one empirical dataset.
methods: Per-loss and aggregate reinsurance transformations; attachment points, limits, stop-loss functions, heavy-tail models and reinsurance pricing.
main_findings: Excess-of-Loss reinsurance produces a nonlinear transformation of gross severities and concentrates sensitivity around attachment and exhaustion points.
limitations: Broad theoretical reference rather than an empirical study of reserve accuracy under volatile inflation or structural change.
how_used_in_dissertation: Foundational source for the per-claim ceded-loss formula, treaty terminology and the explanation of why inflation changes layer entry and exhaustion probabilities.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Reinsurance Literature; Chapter 3 – Treaty Mechanics
notes: Priority: Medium. Target Chapter 2 (reinsurance forms and properties) and Chapter 7 (pricing). Extract exact pages for the layer loss function after accessing the book through the university library.

full_citation: Yeung, K. C. (2011). Index clause for aggregate deductibles and limits in non-proportional reinsurance. Casualty Actuarial Society E-Forum, Spring 2011. https://www.casact.org/sites/default/files/database/forum_11spforum_yeung.pdf
topic: Stability and indexation clauses in non-proportional reinsurance
research_question: How should per-claim and aggregate deductibles and limits be indexed so inflation is shared consistently between cedant, reinsurer and retrocessionaire?
data_used: Mathematical examples and numerical illustrations of indexed non-proportional reinsurance payments.
methods: Deflation of claim payments to a base date; calculation of indexed per-claim deductibles and limits; alternative methods for indexed annual aggregate deductibles and limits.
main_findings: Index or stability clauses preserve the intended economic sharing of an excess layer. Inconsistent indexing of deductibles, limits and aggregate features can materially alter recoveries.
limitations: Focuses on contract mechanics and aggregate features; actual wordings vary and the paper does not compare reserving algorithms.
how_used_in_dissertation: Supports the no-indexation, full-indexation and simplified trigger-based clause scenarios and the consistent adjustment of attachment and limit.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Reinsurance Indexation; Chapter 3 – Contract Scenarios
notes: Priority: High. p. 1 explains the purpose of a stability clause; pp. 2–4 provide the standard calculation and worked example; pp. 6–9 formalise indexed deductible and limit; pp. 25–32 discuss practical implementation and pricing. Clearly label any threshold-trigger clause in the dissertation as a simplified experimental design unless supported by a specific wording.

full_citation: McGuire, G., Taylor, G., & Miller, H. (2021). Self-assembling insurance claim models using regularized regression and machine learning. Variance, 14(1). https://doi.org/10.66573/001c.28366
research_question: Can LASSO regularisation automate flexible reserving GLM construction while retaining interpretable actuarial structure?
data_used: Synthetic triangular data and a real individual-claim dataset with accident, development, calendar and claim-level features.
methods: Penalised GLMs with L1 regularisation; large libraries of basis functions and interactions; standardisation; cross-validation for penalty selection; bootstrap approaches to prediction error.
main_findings: Regularisation can select parsimonious accident-year, development-year, calendar-year and interaction effects from a large candidate library and can identify nonlinear or changing patterns.
limitations: Performance depends on the candidate feature library and validation design. Abrupt changes can be missed, extrapolation requires judgement and the method can be computationally intensive.
how_used_in_dissertation: Primary source for the regularised model’s feature library, L1 penalty, cross-validation and interpretation.
chapter: Chapter 2 – Machine Learning in Reserving; Chapter 3 – Regularised Model
notes: Priority: High. Working-paper pp. 5–8 explain regularisation, LASSO, standardisation and k-fold cross-validation; pp. 13–26 cover feature libraries and applications; pp. 37–38 give conclusions and warn that the method is not an oracle for future inflation or settlement rates and may miss instantaneous changes.

full_citation: Gabrielli, A., Richman, R., & Wüthrich, M. V. (2020). Neural network embedding of the over-dispersed Poisson reserving model. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal, 2020(1), 1–29. https://doi.org/10.1080/03461238.2019.1633394
topic: Neural-network embedding of an actuarial reserving model
research_question: Can a neural network retain a classical over-dispersed Poisson baseline while learning additional nonlinear reserving structure?
data_used: Run-off triangles and simulation examples used to compare the embedded neural network with the classical over-dispersed Poisson model.
methods: Feed-forward neural network nested around the over-dispersed Poisson structure; accident and development effects; nonlinear extensions; bootstrap assessment of prediction uncertainty.
main_findings: Embedding the actuarial model supplies a credible starting point while allowing additional structure to be learned and fitted efficiently.
limitations: Greater complexity, architecture and optimisation sensitivity, reduced interpretability and potentially unstable extrapolation under unprecedented structural change.
how_used_in_dissertation: Primary source for the compact neural-network benchmark and for using an actuarial baseline rather than an unconstrained black-box model.

full_citation: Meyers, G. G., & Shi, P. (2011). The retrospective testing of stochastic loss reserve models. Casualty Actuarial Society E-Forum, Summer 2011. https://www.casact.org/sites/default/files/database/forum_11sumforum_meyers-shi.pdf
topic: Retrospective and diagonal validation of reserving models
research_question: How can predictive distributions from reserving models be tested against outcomes that became observable after the original valuation date?
data_used: NAIC Schedule P paid-loss triangles from 1997 together with subsequent observed development and posted reserves.
methods: Fit models using an earlier valuation triangle; predict the lower triangle; compare predictive distributions and realised outcomes using calibration diagnostics.
main_findings: Reserving models should be evaluated using genuine future observations. Retrospective tests can reveal bias and miscalibration that are hidden by in-sample fit.
limitations: Requires mature historical outcomes and can confound model weakness with environmental change. One historical backtest does not identify performance in every future regime.
how_used_in_dissertation: Justifies rolling-origin or latest-diagonal validation for model and hyperparameter selection rather than random cell splitting.

full_citation: Renshaw, A. E., & Verrall, R. J. (1998). A stochastic model underlying the Chain-Ladder technique. British Actuarial Journal, 4(4), 903–923. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-actuarial-journal/article/stochastic-model-underlying-the-chainladder-technique/B19B65A46F71596963840CF141563C86
topic: Generalised linear model underlying Chain Ladder
research_question: Can the Chain Ladder algorithm be expressed as a statistical model that permits estimation, diagnostics and extensions?
methods: Quasi-likelihood generalised linear model for incremental claims with accident-year and development-year effects.
main_findings: Chain Ladder can be embedded in a GLM framework; this makes its statistical structure explicit and demonstrates that the traditional model is only one narrow member of a wider model class.
limitations: Retains an aggregate triangle structure and does not directly model calendar-year inflation, claim-level reinsurance terms or an unprecedented structural break without extensions.
how_used_in_dissertation: Provides the bridge from classical Chain Ladder to the over-dispersed Poisson and regularised regression formulations.

full_citation: England, P. D., & Verrall, R. J. (2002). Stochastic claims reserving in general insurance. British Actuarial Journal, 8(3), 443–518. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1357321700003809
research_question: How can classical reserving techniques be placed in stochastic frameworks and extended to smoothing, tail extrapolation, Bayesian and bootstrap approaches?
data_used: Illustrative run-off triangles and published reserving examples.
methods: Survey and comparison of stochastic Chain Ladder models, GLMs, parametric curves, smoothing, bootstrap methods and Bornhuetter–Ferguson within Bayesian formulations.
main_findings: Several stochastic models reproduce classical Chain Ladder point estimates while providing different variance assumptions and prediction-error mechanisms. More flexible structures permit smoothing and tail modelling.
limitations: A broad survey rather than a focused study of claims inflation, XoL reinsurance or machine learning under structural change.
how_used_in_dissertation: Provides the general stochastic reserving context and terminology surrounding the selected classical benchmarks.
notes: Priority: Medium. Review the paper’s Sections 2–6 when writing the literature review. Use it as a survey source, while citing primary method papers such as Mack and Renshaw–Verrall for specific formulas.

full_citation: Avanzi, B., Taylor, G., Wang, M., & Wong, B. (2021). SynthETIC: An individual insurance claim simulator with feature control. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics, 100, 296–308. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.insmatheco.2021.06.004
source_type: Peer-reviewed actuarial journal article and open-source simulator
topic: Claim-level simulation with structural feature control
research_question: How can individual claim histories be simulated with controllable occurrence, reporting, settlement, payment, inflation and discontinuity features?
data_used: Synthetic individual claims generated from a modular simulator with user-controlled assumptions.
methods: Simulation of occurrence, notification, settlement, partial payments, claim size, base inflation, superimposed inflation, dependencies and discontinuities; aggregation to triangles.
main_findings: A modular claim-level simulator enables controlled experiments with realistic claim-process features and known ground truth. Inflation can act by calendar or accident period and development or settlement features can change.
limitations: The generated data remain conditional on selected parametric assumptions. Complexity can obscure which mechanism is driving results unless scenarios are carefully isolated.
how_used_in_dissertation: Supports the decision to simulate claims and payments at individual level and then aggregate them, and strengthens the structural-break design.

full_citation: Lloyd’s. (2022). Reserving guidance: Allowing for inflation. https://assets.lloyds.com/media/55a72787-8bca-4516-b508-c88fa0f05670/Reserving-Guidance-Allowing-for-Inflation.pdf
topic: Practical allowance for claims inflation in reserves
research_question: What should managing agents consider when quantifying historical and future claims inflation in reserve estimates?
data_used: Industry guidance based on Lloyd’s market oversight and reserving practice rather than a single statistical dataset.
methods: Assessment of claims frequency and severity; identification of relevant inflation drivers; explicit allowance for inflation already emerged and inflation expected before settlement; sensitivity and scenario analysis.
main_findings: Reserves should reflect both inflation already affecting unsettled claims and forecast inflation through settlement. Analysis should distinguish frequency and severity and consider the duration and persistence of inflation shocks.
limitations: Principles-based guidance rather than a replicable empirical model; firms must select portfolio-specific indices, assumptions and adjustments.
how_used_in_dissertation: Provides direct industry motivation for explicit inflation modelling, cashflow timing and scenario testing.
chapter: Chapter 1 – Motivation; Chapter 2 – Industry Practice; Chapter 5 – Discussion
notes: Priority: High. pp. 2–4 contain the core guidance: separate inflation already emerged from future inflation, analyse frequency and severity, and test the severity and persistence of shocks. Use alongside the 2022 thematic review rather than as evidence of model performance.

full_citation: Wüthrich, M. V. (2018). Machine learning in individual claims reserving. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal, 2018(6), 465–480. https://doi.org/10.1080/03461238.2018.1428681
topic: Machine learning on individual claim histories
research_question: How can machine-learning techniques be used to estimate reserves from individual claim data rather than only aggregate triangles?
methods: Tree-based machine-learning methods applied to individual claim development and payment-count prediction, with aggregation to portfolio reserves.
main_findings: The paper demonstrates the feasibility of using granular claim information for reserving and helped establish the individual-claim ML literature.
limitations: Individual-level methods require granular, consistent data and must still address unreported claims, censoring, extrapolation and validation. One application does not imply universal superiority over aggregate methods.
how_used_in_dissertation: Provides broader ML context and supports retaining claim-level information before triangle aggregation.
notes: Priority: Medium. Obtain the full paper through QMUL access before relying on method details. Use mainly to position the dissertation within the development of granular reserving; the implemented ML models remain triangle/cell based unless the final design is changed.

full_citation: Prudential Regulation Authority. (2023). Follow up to the letter: Insights from PRA thematic review of general insurance reserving and capital modelling. Bank of England. https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/prudential-regulation/letter/2023/june/insights-from-thematic-review.pdf
topic: Claims inflation in reserving, capital and governance
research_question: What weaknesses and good practices did the PRA observe in firms’ treatment of claims inflation in technical provisions, capital models and governance?
data_used: Cross-firm thematic review of UK general insurers, including personal, commercial and London-market business.
methods: Supervisory review of reserve strengthening, inflation assumptions, reinsurance effects, internal models, scenario testing, governance and communication across functions.
main_findings: Persistently elevated claims inflation can affect reserves, own funds and capital simultaneously. Longer-tailed lines may show delayed emergence, and firms should monitor drivers, assumptions, reinsurance basis risk and tail scenarios.
limitations: Supervisory observations are not a controlled statistical experiment and reported market averages should not be transferred directly to the simulated portfolio.
how_used_in_dissertation: Provides regulatory motivation and supports sensitivity testing, long-tail emphasis, reinsurance basis-risk discussion and governance implications.
chapter: Chapter 1 – Motivation; Chapter 2 – Regulatory Context; Chapter 5 – Discussion
notes: Priority: Medium. Review pp. 1–8 for reserve and capital concerns and pp. 13–15 for methodology, reinsurance and internal-model observations. Use for motivation and discussion, not for calibrating simulation parameters.
